question: What simplification does T5 apply to layer normalization?
expected_answer: Activations are rescaled, with no additive bias.

gold.evidence: We use a simplified version of layer normalization where the activations are only rescaled and no additive bias is applied.

question: How are relative position embeddings simplified in the T5 implementation?
expected_answer: Each position embedding is a scalar added to the attention logit.

gold.evidence: We use a simplified form of position embeddings where each “embedding” is simply a scalar that is added to the corresponding logit used for computing the attention weights.

question: What minimum sentence and word counts were required when cleaning Common Crawl for C4?
expected_answer: Discard pages with fewer than five sentences; retain lines with at least three words.

gold.evidence: We discarded any page with fewer than 5 sentences and only retained lines that contained at least 3 words.

question: Approximately how large is the cleaned English C4 corpus described in the paper?

gold.evidence: This produces a collection of text that is not only orders of magnitude larger than most data sets used for pre-training (about 750 GB) but also comprises reasonably clean and natural English text.

question: Within the Setup section, how does the text-to-text model know which task to perform?
expected_answer: A task-specific text prefix is added to the original input sequence.

gold.evidence: To specify which task the model should perform, we add a task-specific (text) prefix to the original input sequence before feeding it to the model.

question: How does T5 turn an STS-B similarity score such as 2.57 into a text target?
expected_answer: Round to the nearest 0.2, so 2.57 becomes the string 2.6.

gold.evidence: We found that most of these scores were annotated in increments of 0.2, so we simply rounded any score to the nearest increment of 0.2 and converted the result to a literal string representation of the number (e.g. the floating-point value 2.57 would be mapped to the string “2.6”).

question: Which optimizer and test-time decoding method does the baseline use?

gold.evidence: For optimization, we use AdaFactor (Shazeer and Stern, 2018). At test time, we use greedy decoding (i.e. choosing the highest-probability logit at every timestep).

question: What tokenizer and vocabulary size are used across the experiments?

gold.evidence: We use SentencePiece (Kudo and Richardson, 2018) to encode text as WordPiece tokens (Sennrich et al., 2015; Kudo, 2018). For all experiments, we use a vocabulary of 32,000 wordpieces.

question: What character caused C4 cleaning to discard a page because it could indicate code?

gold.evidence: we removed any pages that contained a curly bracket.

question: What fraction of input tokens does the baseline denoising objective drop, and how are consecutive dropped spans represented?
expected_answer: Drop 15% of tokens; replace each consecutive span with one sentinel token.

gold.evidence: we design an objective that randomly samples and then drops out 15% of tokens in the input sequence. All consecutive spans of dropped-out tokens are replaced by a single sentinel token.

question: How did sharing encoder-decoder parameters compare with halving their numbers of layers?
expected_answer: Sharing performed nearly as well, while halving the layers significantly hurt performance.

gold.evidence: Surprisingly, we found that sharing parameters across the encoder and decoder performed nearly as well. In contrast, halving the number of layers in the encoder and decoder stacks significantly hurt performance.

question: Which average corrupted span length slightly outperformed independent corruption on most non-translation benchmarks?

gold.evidence: We also find in particular that using an average span length of 3 slightly (but significantly) outperforms the i.i.d. objective on most non-translation benchmarks.

question: Why do the authors suspect that shrinking the pre-training dataset can hurt downstream performance?
expected_answer: The model may memorize the smaller pre-training dataset.

gold.evidence: As expected, performance degrades as the data set size shrinks. We suspect this may be due to the fact that the model begins to memorize the pre-training data set.

question: What explanations are offered for the poor performance of equal task mixing?
expected_answer: Low-resource tasks may overfit, high-resource tasks may see too little data, or the model may see too little unlabeled data.

gold.evidence: The “equal” mixing strategy in particular results in dramatically degraded performance, which may be because the low-resource tasks have overfit, the high-resource tasks have not seen enough data, or the model has not seen enough unlabeled data to learn general-purpose language capabilities.

question: How does the scaling experiment combine model outputs in an ensemble?
expected_answer: Average logits before the output softmax to obtain an aggregate prediction.

gold.evidence: We average the logits across the ensemble before feeding them into the output softmax nonlinearity to obtain an aggregate prediction.

question: Which weights are shared with the input embedding matrix in the decoder?
expected_answer: The weights of the dense layer with softmax output.

gold.evidence: The output of the final decoder block is fed into a dense layer with a softmax output, whose weights are shared with the input embedding matrix.

question: What minimum English classification probability did C4 filtering require?

gold.evidence: we used langdetect7 to filter out any pages that were not classified as English with a probability of at least 0.99.

question: Which ROUGE metric is reported for CNN/Daily Mail in the main tables?

gold.evidence: For CNN/Daily Mail, we find the performance of models on the ROUGE-1-F, ROUGE-2-F, and ROUGE-L-F metrics (Lin, 2004) to be highly correlated so we report the ROUGE-2-F score alone under the heading “CNNDM”.

question: In the BERT-style objective described, what fraction of corrupted tokens are replaced by a random token?

gold.evidence: 90% of the corrupted tokens are replaced with a special mask token and 10% are replaced with a random token.

question: How large was the resulting WebText-like dataset?

gold.evidence: This produced a 17 GB WebText-like data set
